rv.q: The Upstart Crow is, theatrically, the definite article.
At the Gielgud (mark thee, formerly The Globe), the laughter is communal and continual.
Upstart Crow is more accurate about Shakespeare than you might think
Fast, often escalating into delirious silliness, Upstart Crow must be deemed a hit, a hit, an implausible hit.
Fans are in for a treat, as it's basically a bumper episode, with most of the cast reprising their turns.
The result is an affectionate Shakespeare send-up: enjoyably daft and unashamedly crowd-pleasing.
Elton interlocks the plots in really clever ways, and there are loads of good gags, but the show as a whole feels like little more than the sum of its pilfered parts.
The pleasures of the series are here too, though, with plenty of giggles for the Bard-literate.

Toss in some agreeable silliness with a man in a bear suit, a wonderful turn from Mark Heap as a self-denying Puritan, and a fistful of genuinely good gags and you have a fun night, smoothly directed by stage-comedy supremo Sean Foley.
That said, the relentlessly full-tilt, neon-bright, selfie-snapping teenager world is cartoonish and won’t appeal to everyone.
The elevated silliness of Elton’s many-layered plot is superbly handled.
This play – like the TV sitcom from which it sprang – deserves the love lavished upon it.
Still, the action doesn't get going until the second half, too many jokes fall flat and there is a slight whiff of money for old rope.

cn.t: Elton's sitcom-to-stage adaptation delights fans with its silly, affectionate send-up of Shakespeare, buoyed by Mitchell's crowd-pleasing performance, though some find the lowbrow humor repetitive over two-plus hours.
